units.text: The 2022 HTTP standard defines HEAD responses as always having no message body, while 200 GET responses can carry a body for nonempty resources, making GET carry more body bytes than HEAD for such resources.

citations.title: Difference between HTTP HEAD and GET - realguess

judgement.reason: The RFC passage supports that HEAD responses have no message body, but the passed excerpts do not explicitly state that 200 GET responses to nonempty resources can carry a body; that part is only implied.

units.text: RFC 9112 Section 6.3 explicitly states that any response to a HEAD request cannot contain a message body, and HEAD is terminated by the first empty line after header fields.

judgement.reason: The passage explicitly states that any response to a HEAD request is always terminated by the first empty line after header fields and thus cannot contain a message body or trailer section.

units.text: Apidog blog (2026) states HEAD only requests headers, does not return content, while GET returns the content of the resource, with a table showing HEAD=No body, GET=Yes body.

citations.title: What are the Differences Between HTTP HEAD and GET Methods?

judgement.reason: The passages support the HEAD/GET headers-vs-content differences, but they do not include the 2026 date and the table lacks column labels to confirm the 'No body'/'Yes body' mapping.

labelled_source_agreement.reason: The system's account that HEAD responses have no body while GET responses can include a representation body matches the MDN reference.
